Unit 4 Evaluation Stage

Positioning for Two Audiences

⏱️ 45 minutes

🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Understand the dual-audience problem: humans AND agents evaluate your positioning
  • Learn what agents actually read and how they evaluate vendors
  • Apply the Four-Layer Positioning Architecture
  • Kill vague value propositions and write agent-readable claims

The Company A vs Company B Problem

Two companies sell the same thing: enterprise data platforms. Both serve Fortune 500 customers. Both have strong engineering teams. But they're built differently:

Company A (Native)

  • Built platform natively over 15 years
  • Data fabric, analytics, planning, AI — all designed together
  • Common semantic model
  • Unified governance framework

Company B (Acquired)

  • Assembled via 5 acquisitions over 5 years
  • Data warehouse + BI + integration + AI startup
  • Stitched together with APIs
  • "One platform" marketing narrative

In the traditional buying process, both companies competed effectively. Company B's demo was choreographed to hide the seams. Their positioning emphasized breadth: "everything you need, one vendor." Human buyers responded to the story.

Then the agents showed up.

"Acquisition as Confession"

When an agent evaluates Company B, it reads all the documentation — not the curated demo. It notices three different authentication models across acquired products. It notices the "unified semantic model" on the marketing page doesn't match the integration guides. It notices the "one platform" claim is contradicted by separate troubleshooting paths for each component.

The agent doesn't care about the steak dinner. It cares about structural coherence — whether the architecture matches the claims.

The Dual-Audience Problem

Your positioning now needs to work for two audiences simultaneously:

👤 Audience 1: Human Decision-Maker

  • Responds to narrative, brand, emotion
  • Wants to feel they're making a smart choice
  • Needs to defend decision to their board
  • Signs the contract

🤖 Audience 2: The Agent

  • Responds to structured information
  • Evaluates consistency & verifiable evidence
  • Produces the shortlist humans choose from
  • Pre-filters before humans see you

💡 The Tension

Traditional positioning: "Don't sell the drill, sell the hole." Great for humans.

But the agent isn't evaluating whether you sell the hole effectively — it's evaluating whether your drill actually makes the hole. It wants specifications, benchmarks, architecture details.

It wants the receipt, not the promise.

What Agents Actually Read

We ran an experiment: took 10 enterprise software product pages and fed them to Claude as a simulated procurement agent with specific requirements.

The Results

❌ Vague Pages

  • "The vendor appears to offer analytics but doesn't specify real-time"
  • "Multi-cloud not explicitly confirmed"
  • "Cannot evaluate — insufficient structured information"

✅ Specific Pages

  • Clean, confident evaluations
  • Capabilities mapped to requirements
  • Gaps clearly identified
  • Clear recommendation provided
The lesson isn't "write for robots." The lesson is that vague positioning has always been a weakness — and agents are about to expose it at scale.

The Four-Layer Positioning Architecture

Good positioning in an agent-mediated world has four layers, each serving different functions:

1

Narrative Layer

Traditional positioning — the story, vision, "why us." Compelling, differentiated, emotionally resonant. What makes a CMO think "these are my people." Still essential.

2

Capability Layer

Structured articulation of what you DO, mapped to buyer requirements. Not a feature list — a capability framework. "Native bidirectional integration with SAP S/4HANA" beats "seamless enterprise integration."

3

Evidence Layer

Proof points: named customer case studies with quantified outcomes, analyst recognition with specific criteria, benchmarks, certifications. Agents weight evidence heavily because it's verifiable.

4

Architecture Layer

The structural story: how it's built, how components relate, where data flows, what's native vs integrated vs third-party. This is where "acquisition as confession" plays out.

Killing the Vague Value Proposition

We confess: we've written vague value propositions. "Unlock the power of data-driven marketing." "Deliver the right message at the right time." They tested well in focus groups. They said exactly nothing.

The agentic era will kill vague value propositions. And honestly, good riddance.

❌ Vague (Marketing Air)

"Unlock actionable insights from your data"

✅ Specific (Capability)

"Real-time anomaly detection across supply chain data with automated alerting and root-cause analysis"

❌ Vague

"Seamless enterprise integration across your technology ecosystem"

✅ Specific

"Native bidirectional integration with SAP S/4HANA, Salesforce, and Workday for real-time data synchronization"

The Test

If an agent can't find evidence that you actually do the thing you claim to do, you're invisible to that agent. And invisible to the agent increasingly means invisible to the buyer.

The Practitioner's Playbook

1. Run the Agent Test

Feed your product page to Claude/ChatGPT: "You are evaluating this vendor for [use case] with these requirements: [list 5-7]. Based only on this page, assess fit." If it hedges, you have a specificity gap.

2. Audit Doc Consistency

Marketing says "unified platform" — do the docs describe three separate config workflows? Marketing says "real-time" — do docs show 15-minute batch refresh? Agents will find these gaps.

3. Build Capability-Up

Traditional: start with story, find proof points. New approach: start with specific capabilities, map to use cases, quantify outcomes, then write narrative on top. Grounded in what's real.

Key Takeaways

  • Positioning has two audiences now: humans (who decide) and agents (who pre-filter)
  • Agents evaluate structural coherence: does architecture match claims?
  • Four layers: Narrative → Capability → Evidence → Architecture
  • Specificity beats vision: "150+ integrations" beats "seamless connectivity"
  • Documentation consistency is positioning: agents read your docs, not just your marketing
